 Rare Unilateral Neuroretinitis Linked to Dengue Infection in Returning Traveller
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 A 33-year-old man experienced unilateral neuroretinitis and acute visual loss in his right eye following a febrile illness contracted during travel to Thailand, according to a case report published in the Journal of Ophthalmic Inflammation and Infection. While ocular manifestations of dengue are well recognized in clinical practice, they typically occur bilaterally, making isolated unilateral presentation an uncommon medical finding.
 Initial ophthalmic examination of the patient’s affected right eye revealed unilateral optic disc oedema, vitritis, retinal haemorrhages, and retinal thickening involving the macula. High-resolution optical coherence tomography demonstrated marked serous retinal detachment accompanied by significant central retinal thickening.
 Fluorescein angiography confirmed optic disc and retinal vascular leakage consistent with active neuroretinitis and retinal vasculitis in the right eye. An extensive panel of neurological and infectious work-ups systematically excluded other potential causes of neuroretinitis, while serological testing confirmed a diagnostic profile consistent with recent dengue infection.
 Following clinical exclusion of the active phase of the viral infection, the patient received treatment with systemic corticosteroids. The therapy prompted rapid anatomical improvement and substantial visual recovery, with the visual gains remaining stable throughout long-term follow-up evaluations.
 The study authors highlighted that dengue-associated neuroretinitis can manifest unilaterally and emphasized that clinicians should include dengue infection in the differential diagnosis of posterior segment ocular inflammation in returning travellers, even during atypical presentations.
 In evaluating the investigative design, the authors framed their findings as a brief report focused on an individual patient. Because the evidence stems from a single case, the study cannot measure the broader incidence or determine precise risk factors for unilateral ocular involvement across all travelers exposed to dengue. Instead, the documentation demonstrates that unilateral manifestation is a documented possibility despite the typical bilateral pattern observed in medical practice.
 By conducting an extensive neurological and infectious investigation, the medical team ruled out competing etiologies, ensuring that the inflammatory condition was properly linked to the recent viral episode. 
 Subject of Research: Unilateral neuroretinitis following recent dengue infection in a returning traveller
 Article Title: Unilateral dengue-associated neuroretinitis: a case report
